o: A substring is balanced when every distinct character in it occurs the same number of times; note a single distinct character trivially qualifies, so the answer is at least the longest run of one letter. For "abbac" the answer is "abba" (a and b twice); for "aabcc" it is "abc"; for "aba" it is any length-2 pair. With n up to 1e5 we need better than O(n^2): the classic tool is prefix-count signatures hashed to the first occurrence, applied once for the 3-letter case and once per 2-letter pair (excluding the third letter).
k: For all-three-equal, hash the pair (cnt_a - cnt_b, cnt_b - cnt_c); a repeated signature marks a balanced substring.
For each pair (x,y), restrict to segments between occurrences of the third letter z and hash cnt_x - cnt_y; a repeat inside a segment gives a balanced substring using exactly x and y.
A zero difference over a non-empty segment with only x,y present forces both counts positive, so no extra presence check is needed.
Any single character is balanced, so initialize the answer to 1.

a.i: Fix every start index, extend the end while maintaining the three counts, and test balance. Direct translation of the definition; too slow for n = 1e5 but a correct baseline.
s: For each start i, reset counts and scan forward.
Track how many distinct characters are present.
If all present counts are equal, update the answer with the current length.
a.t: O(n^2) - all O(n^2) substrings evaluated with O(1) updates

a.i: Balance is a condition on count differences, and differences compose additively across a substring, so 'substring has equal counts' becomes 'two prefixes share the same signature'. Handle the 3-character case with the pair (a-b, b-c), and each 2-character pair inside segments delimited by the excluded letter.
s: Scan once storing the first index of each (cnt_a-cnt_b, cnt_b-cnt_c) signature; on a repeat update the answer.
For each ordered choice of pair (x,y) and excluded letter z, scan again: reset the difference map whenever z appears, store first index of cnt_x - cnt_y, and on repeats update the answer.
Initialize the answer to 1 for single-character substrings.
a.t: O(n log n) - four linear scans with logarithmic map operations (O(n) with hash maps)

w: Present the signature approach; it generalizes the classic 'equal 0s and 1s' trick. Pitfalls: forgetting single-character substrings are balanced, forgetting to reset the pair maps at each occurrence of the excluded letter, and assuming a zero difference implies both letters appear (true only because the segment is non-empty and contains no third letter). Follow-up: k distinct characters, or counting balanced substrings instead of the longest.
